One Index, Two Markets

Burst Monitor · the read from the Friday, October 30 close

One Index, Two Markets

On Friday the S&P 500 had its worst day since June. The typical stock inside it lost a quarter of a percent. That gap is not a one-day quirk. Since the index set a record on October 6 it has fallen 3% while most of its members have risen, the typical one by 5%. An instrument built to watch how the five hundred move together has been tracking this split since July. Here is what it saw on Friday, in plain terms, and what it is waiting to see next.

If you are new here · the story so far, in three lines

Since July
When the S&P 500 moves, its stocks usually move together: an up day lifts nearly all of them. Since July the biggest shared move has instead been two-sided: one group of stocks rising while another falls. The record going back to 2000 has nothing like it for longer than a few weeks. This is month four.
October 6 → 23
The index made a record on October 6 carried by its largest names. Over the next two weeks the rally rotated away from them: the AI complex (Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta, Alphabet, and the names that trade with them) fell while most other stocks rose. On October 21 the instrument fixed the two groups by name so that nothing could be re-sorted after the fact. Earlier reads told that story as it formed; Two Bodies (Oct 26) tells it end to end.
This week
The index's worst day since June landed on the group that was already falling. The question this edition answers is what Friday changed, and the answer is: less than the headline suggests, in a market that is still two markets.

1 · Whose bad day

The index fell 1.8%. The typical stock fell a quarter of a point.

Friday was the S&P 500's third-worst session of 2026 and its worst since June 5. It was not a stampede. Line the five hundred stocks up by what they did on Friday and the one in the middle lost 0.25%. The damage was concentrated: in technology, and above all in the AI complex, with the index's ten largest names at the center of it.

The reason a mild day for the typical stock can be a bad day for the index is arithmetic. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted: each company counts in proportion to its market value, so the ten largest names, 37% of the index at current prices, move it more than the other four hundred and ninety together can. All ten fell on Friday, by 1.5% at the median. Most of the market did not.

Hold the two groups the instrument fixed on October 21 and the day reads cleanly. The crest 315, the stocks that had rallied through October, finished up 0.30% at the median, with 184 of the 315 higher. The trough 115, the AI complex and the names that trade with it, fell 2.35% at the median, with 92 of the 115 lower. By sector the day ran from technology at −4.1% to consumer staples at +1.6% and energy at +1.6%, with utilities and materials also up. (The names of the two groups come from the instrument's clock face, chapter 4: the crest is the group just past the top of its swing that day, the trough the group at the bottom.)

The week, day by day

each session's return: the index, the median stock of all 501, the crest 315 and the trough 115 · the label over each day is the share of the 501 that rose

Friday also undid the week's first half. Monday through Wednesday the trough bounced (+1.0%, +1.9% and +0.3% at the median) while the crest drifted, and the index rose on the bounce. Thursday was the mirror: Alphabet fell 12.6% after its results and the ten lost 1.4% at the median, yet 81% of the five hundred rose, so the index slipped while its typical stock gained 1.5%. Friday took the trough's bounce back. Over the five sessions the two groups ended almost level, crest +1.27% and trough +1.16% at the median. The index lost 0.57% because its ten largest names lost 1.94%.

The split since August 13

the median of each group's return since Aug 13, with the S&P 500 and the median of all 501 · gold ticks = closure days, explained in chapter 3 · the dashed line is the Oct 6 record

Since the record the gap is wide. From October 6 the index is down 3.05% while its median stock is up 5.44%. The crest 315 is up 8.85% at the median, with 91% of its members higher. The trough 115 is down 9.41%, and the ten largest are down 13.85%. An index with 37% of its value in ten names that have fallen 14% can lose ground while most of its members rise, and for four weeks it has. That is the sense in which there is one index and two markets.

Outside the instrument · the analyst's layer, kept separate

The instrument reads prices only, by design. Its job is to say where the pressure and the coordination are, not why. Everything below this line is the analyst's: dated facts, an explanation they are compatible with, and what would weaken it.

The facts, dated against the sessions. Wednesday Oct 28, 2:00 pm ET: the Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75–4.00% by a 10–2 vote; both dissenters wanted an increase. Wednesday after the close: Alphabet reported revenue up 25% and Google Cloud up 103%, with capital spending of $51.4B against $42.3B of operating cash flow, a second straight quarter of negative free cash flow. Microsoft reported revenue up 19% and Azure up 48%. Thursday after the close: Amazon reported AWS up 39% and a trailing-year cash outflow of $42B, with the jump in equipment spending attributed "primarily" to AI. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue below the third's and said it expects the PC slowdown to last at least through mid-2027.

A compatible explanation. Thursday was the first session after Alphabet's and Microsoft's reports; Friday the first after Amazon's and Intel's. A reassessment of what the AI build-out costs, and when it pays, fits the shape: the losses landed on the hardware and megacap side while the same releases reported strong cloud demand. Intel's PC outlook is a narrower channel into the hardware names. A Fed leaning toward higher rates is a broader backdrop.

What would weaken it. Similarly exposed names that did not report holding up while the reporters fell. Unrelated groups beginning to fall just as hard. The breadth of the week argues against a single macro story: 81% of names up on Thursday, the crest higher on Friday, energy and staples higher. And none of it explains the split itself, which began in July, months before these reports.

2 · What the split is

One shared move, long one side and short the other

The instrument's first job is to say how the five hundred move together. Its simplest reading takes every stock's daily return over the last 21 sessions and asks what the single biggest shared pattern is. In a normal market that pattern is "the market": on an up day nearly every stock rises, and 99 of 100 names sit on the same side of it. Since July the biggest shared pattern has been two-sided, one block of stocks rising while another falls. On Friday's reading 75 of 100 share its sign; a quarter of the market is on the other leg.

Two words carry this chapter. The first direction is that biggest shared pattern. The same-sign share is the fraction of stocks on the same side of it: 99% is a market moving as one; 75% is a long-short pattern. On the instrument's slow reader, which uses 63 sessions, the share has been under 85% for 82 straight sessions, since July 8. In the 26 years before, the longest such run was 17 sessions, in February 2001. Whatever this is, the record has no precedent for its length.

A second reading counts how many separate things are going on. The story count is the effective number of independent directions in those same returns: twenty would mean twenty separate stories, and a count collapsing toward three or four means one move has taken over, which is what the market looked like on the way into 2008, March 2020 and the spring of 2025. That is why the board is watched for a storm when the count falls. Since October 14 the fast reader has fallen 39%, from 13.6 to 8.3. Jason's first note from the board on Sunday: pressure toward the storm side; not there, but trending that way.

The story count since August, with Friday computed in

21-session reader (ink) and 63-session reader (gold), by morning · hollow markers = the window that ends on Friday, computed now · × = what Friday alone would have done

But look at what the fall is made of. Since October 14 the first direction has grown, from 17% of the variation to 29%, while its same-sign share has fallen, from 90% to 75%. The market is using fewer independent directions because it has organized more strongly into opposition, not because it has become one. Fewer stories because two bodies got louder.

What the fall is made of

21-session reader: the first direction's share of the variation (ink) and the second's (gold), left scale · the first direction's same-sign share (teal), right scale · hollow markers = the window ending Friday

Friday's own move is not yet in the board's reading: each morning's reading is built from returns through the session before. But every return the next window needs is already in hand, so it can be computed now rather than waited for. With Friday in, the count slips from 8.29 to 8.22, and that slip is October 1 leaving the window; on its own Friday would have nudged the count up, to 8.64, one more session that did not ride the main direction. The same-sign share does not move. Friday, the worst index day since June, left the market no more unified than it found it.

Which direction did Friday travel? Among the two leading patterns, Friday lined up more with the second, which leans on the trough names, than with the first: 15% of the day's shape against 10% on the fast reader, 27% against 8% on the slow one. Most of the day lies outside both, as most days do. For contrast, October 22, the day after Meta's report, was a first-direction day, with 55% of its shape along the main split. Friday was not the split tightening. It was the other crowd having its own bad day.

The story count fell because the market organized into opposition. Friday's selling did not turn that opposition into one direction.

3 · Where the pressure went

The side that rallied is under pressure. The side that fell has stepped out.

The instrument's clearest picture of two markets is not a number. It is a map. Through early October the whole field was quiet. Then, over eleven straight sessions, the stocks that had rallied were pulled into the market's shared motion while the AI complex stayed outside it. On Friday the group that fell hardest was the group that had already stepped out.

The motion map places each stock by two things. Vertically, its pressure: how much of its movement is the market's shared movement, measured against that stock's own normal. The white line is the floor, normal; below the floor is above-normal pressure, a stock caught up in what everyone is doing; above it is a stock moving on its own. Horizontally, how tightly it tracks the index. Pressure is refilled by a closure: a session on which at least 8% of the instrument's pool, 51 names, reach the top of their own swings together, a shared crest. Between closures, pressure decays, with a half-life of 21 sessions.

Pressure by body, May to October

the average position on the map's vertical axis for the crest 315 (gold) and the trough 115 (blue), in today's drawing · below 0 is below the floor, under above-normal pressure · gold ticks = closure days · hover for how many of each group sit below the floor

The two bodies ran together through the summer and into October. By October 9 only 8 of the 501 names sat below the floor; both groups were floating high and quiet, as a market does in a long stretch without a shared crest. Then the closures came: eleven in a row, October 15 through 29, every one of them led by the crest. Each pulled more of the rallying side below the floor. By Friday 243 of the 315 crest names were under above-normal pressure. Three of the 115 trough names were. The AI complex never joined: 112 of the 115 sit above the floor, and 49 of them are in the map's breakaway corner, quiet and uncoupled from the index at once: Micron, Applied Materials, KLA, Marvell and both Alphabet lines among them.

This is the part of Friday that a breadth statistic cannot show. The stocks that fell hardest were not being dragged down by the market; they were moving on their own, and had been for weeks. The stocks under the market's shared pressure are the ones that rallied. An empty strain corner with a populated breakaway corner is not calm; it is dispersion. One body is coordinated, and it is not the body that had the bad day.

4 · Two crowds on the clock

Most of the market just past a top; the giants just past a bottom, provisionally

The dial on the first page puts every stock on a clock face by where it is in its own swing. On Friday nearly half the index's value sat just past the top of its swing and four tenths sat just past the bottom: two crowds, half a cycle apart, with most of the giants in the second. The shape is steady. The giants' exact position against the bottom is the softest number on the board, and this chapter shows how soft.

The Phase Dial reads each stock's price against its own 20-session average and turns the result into a position in a swing. Twelve o'clock, home, is a stock that has just finished a run up relative to its average. The right-hand side is the roll down. Six o'clock, the trough, is a stock that has just finished a run down. The left-hand side is the climb back. Motion is clockwise. A group's hand is its average position, with a strength from 0 (spread all around the face) to 1 (all in one place); below about 0.35 a hand is not a position. Two cautions belong beside every reading. A position is not a price direction: the ten fell 1.5% on the day they printed past the bottom. And the newest day's dot is a sketch, for a reason explained below.

Inside Friday's film the motion is clockwise for 448 of the 501 names. About 85 crossed the top into the upper-right crowd. About 40, carrying 29% of the displayed value, crossed the bottom into the lower-left: Nvidia, Amazon, both Alphabet lines, Broadcom and Micron among them. The market's own hand sits just past the top and beginning to roll down, at 0.16 of a cycle with strength 0.43, what the board calls the descending flank. That reading belongs to the big crest crowd (its hand 0.16, strength 0.78) and it has been stable from print to redraw. The trough 115 as a whole is doing the opposite of tightening: its strength fell from 0.59 on Thursday's print to 0.47 on Friday's, even as its giants bunched together at the bottom.

Where the ten largest sit in their swings

each row a cap line · hollow ring = Thursday's own morning print · small gray dot = Thursday as redrawn once Friday was added · filled dot = Friday's print · the clock runs left to right: top of the swing, roll down, bottom, climb back

Now the caution. Each stock's position is computed from its whole price history, and the newest day has nothing after it. When Monday's close arrives, every position is recomputed, and Friday's dot moves. The chart above shows it happening once: the hollow rings are where the giants printed on Thursday morning; the gray dots are where Thursday sits now that Friday has been added. Nvidia printed at .61 on Thursday, past the bottom. Redrawn, Thursday's Nvidia is at .45, still on the way down. Then Friday's print put it past the bottom again, at .56.

The same print, eight mornings running

for each morning since the groups were fixed: the share of the index's value the dial printed just past the bottom (filled gold), and the share today's redrawing of that same morning shows there (hollow) · the labels count how many of the ten largest were past the bottom, printed and redrawn

Every morning since October 21, the dial has printed the giants past the bottom of their swings. Every redraw so far has put them back on the way down. Eight mornings running, between four and seven of the ten largest names printed just past the bottom; in today's drawing of those same mornings, none to three of them are there, and Nvidia is on none of the first seven. The same thing in aggregate: each morning printed roughly 40% of the index's value past the bottom, and today's redrawing of those mornings shows 8% to 29%.

That is the record of the last eight mornings, not a prediction of the ninth; the instrument's own rule is that an observed lean at the edge is not permission to assume the next revision. What it does settle is how to read Friday's dial. The two-crowd shape, with most of the market just past a top and rolling, is firm. Whether the giants have reached the bottom of their own swings is the one thing on this page to hold loosely until Tuesday morning's build, the first to add a new session after Friday. If it holds there, it will be the first time since the groups were fixed that it has.

The same caution, on the closure count · Thursday's 43 became 131

The shared crests of chapter 3 are read from the same positions, so they move the same way. Thursday morning's print had 43 of the 501 shown at home together, just over the line. The read written on Friday morning, before Friday's prices existed, called that the redraw would put more than 43 at home with a crest majority; it came back with 131, 99 of them crest. Friday's own print is quiet: 40 on the instrument's ledger, below the 51 needed, with 26 of the 501 at home, 12 crest and 5 trough. Whether Friday becomes a closure, and whose, is open. Every closure in the current run has been led by the crest; one led by the trough would be new.

5 · Which past

Two memories, nearly tied, with a valley between them

The last reading has a time dimension. Every morning the instrument asks over what lookback the market's shared energy is most tightly organized against its drawdown from the high: how far back the market is remembering. Two answers are nearly tied, and control has passed between them three times this month.

The sweep runs from 60 sessions to six years. At each lookback it measures how strongly the shared energy and the drawdown move together, letting one lead the other by up to 180 sessions. Where the relationship is strongly positive the two are coupled at that memory length; where negative, anti-coupled. The winning lookback is the market's working memory for the day, and the board draws a five-morning median of the winners as the settled reach. On Friday the profile has two coupled ridges, at about ten months (204 sessions, +0.91) and about nineteen months (408 sessions, +0.89). The gap between them is .019, close enough that small shifts in where a ridge's center is detected decide the winner. The settled reach ran at 384 into mid-October, 204 from October 15 to 21, 396 from October 22 to 28, and 204 again on Thursday and Friday: the zigzag Jason circled on the settlement line.

The memory profile on Friday

the relationship at each lookback, Oct 30 (ink) and Oct 23 (faint gold) · open rings = cells whose best lead or lag sits at the ±180 edge of the search, timing unresolved · shaded = the anti-coupled valley · below 130 sessions the instrument's floor

Between the ridges, at roughly thirteen to fifteen months, the sign flips: a valley where the shared energy runs against the drawdown, with the energy lagging. That is the configuration Jason reads on the boundary map as a warning, "pay attention, the downside just opened", and the rust that re-formed deeper on that map this week is this valley. But across most of it the best alignment sits at the very edge of what the sweep can see, so its timing is unresolved. It is a mark to watch, not that configuration confirmed. One further mark for the record: at the 378-session horizon a long-standing floor-loss signature was joined on Friday's build by a correlation-flip signature; across the full lead-lag window the relationship there is still positive, about +0.80, weakened rather than inverted, and it has not yet run its persistence check.

6 · What would change this read

Three branches, and the four things that will tell them apart

The board does not have a direction this week. It has two crowds in opposition, a story count that fell through that opposition rather than through unification, pressure on the side that rallied, and giants that have printed past the bottom of their swings eight mornings in a row without a redraw agreeing. Here are the three ways it can go, and what would distinguish them.

Branch 1Still two markets

The first direction stays two-sided (same-sign share under 85%) while the story count stays low; the two crowds hold half a cycle apart; closures keep coming from the crest side. Rotation, month four. Friday's computed window is consistent with this branch so far.

Branch 2One market

The same-sign share climbs back toward 95% while the first direction's share grows; the crowds converge on the dial and the whole market's hand strengthens past 0.55; the slow reader starts falling with the fast one. That is the shape the record's storms had on the way in. Friday did not move toward it.

Branch 3The opposition fades

The second direction keeps absorbing days like Friday's; the first direction's share falls back; the trough crowd keeps spreading out (strength under 0.4) rather than turning together; the fast reader recovers. The split dissolves instead of resolving.
  1. Monday's return, as soon as it is in.now: the window ending Friday reads 8.22 · first direction 28%, second 15%, same-sign 75%

    Monday's session can be computed the moment its close exists. Does it ride the first direction (the split), the second (the trough's own), or neither? The same arithmetic as chapter 2.

  2. The giants, on Tuesday morning's build.now: Nvidia .56, Amazon .56, Broadcom .56, Micron .57, Alphabet .60, Meta .61 · printed past the bottom eight mornings running, redrawn back seven times

    Tuesday's build is the first to add a new session after Friday. Do the giants stay past the bottom of their swings, or redraw back before it, as every morning so far has? And does the trough 115's hand (0.47) keep loosening while the ten's (0.58) holds?

  3. Whose closure Friday becomes.now: 40 on the ledger, a quiet day · 26 of the 501 at home: crest 12, trough 5

    If Friday's quiet print revises into a shared crest, read who is at home. The crest again is the episode so far. The trough for the first time would be new.

  4. Which memory holds.now: 204 sessions at +.908, 408 at +.889 · the gap .019

    Does the ten-month ridge open its lead, or do two more 408 mornings move the settled reach back? Does the valley's timing come off the edge of the search?

Interpretation

  • The story count fell through opposition, not unification.
  • Friday's damage concentrated on the side that had already stepped out of the market's shared motion.
  • The two-crowd shape is firm; the giants' crossing of the bottom is not.
  • The settled reach's zigzag is control changing hands between two surviving ridges.
  • An AI-cost reassessment as the reason is the analyst's reading, not a measurement.

Not established

  • A direction, a mechanism, a forecast.
  • That the giants have turned.
  • How far Friday's dots will move on Tuesday, for any name.
  • That the valley's timing is real.
  • That Friday becomes a closure, or whose.
  • That any outside event caused the split.

The instrument's words

A short glossary

The crest 315 · the trough 115
The two groups the dial placed just past the top and at the bottom of their swings on October 21, held fixed by name since. The trough holds the AI complex: Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta, Alphabet and the names that trade with them. Amazon is in the crest.
The ten
The ten largest cap lines among the names shown: nine companies, Alphabet twice. About 37% of the value shown, at current prices.
First direction · same-sign share
The biggest shared pattern in the stocks' daily returns over a window, and the fraction of stocks on the same side of it. 99% is a market moving as one; 75% is a long-short pattern with a quarter of the market on the other leg.
The story count
The effective number of independent directions in those returns: the fast reader uses 21 sessions, the slow reader 63. Each morning's reading uses returns through the session before, so a day's own move enters the next morning.
The map · pressure · the floor · breakaway
Each stock's participation in the market's shared moves against its own normal (vertical) and how tightly it tracks the index (horizontal). Below the floor is above-normal pressure. Breakaway is the corner for names that are both quiet and uncoupled. Pressure decays on a 21-session half-life unless a closure refills it.
A closure
A session on which at least 8% of the instrument's pool, 51 names, reach the top of their own swings together: a shared crest. The newest day's count is a sketch and has been revising upward.
The dial · home · the trough · hand
Each stock's price against its own 20-session average, read as a position in a swing. Home is the top, the trough the bottom, motion clockwise. A group's hand is its average position with a strength from 0 to 1; below 0.35 it is not a position. A position is not a price direction.
A print · a redraw
The morning's reading of the newest day is its print. When the next session arrives every position is recomputed, and that day's new reading is its redraw. Both are kept, and this edition says which one it quotes.
The memory · settled reach · coupled
The lookback at which the market's shared energy is most tightly organized against its drawdown, and the five-morning median of the daily winners. Coupled is a positive relationship, anti-coupled a negative one; lag means the energy follows the price.
